lines.text: More than three hundred islands in the South Pacific, settled by bold voyagers and shaped by chiefs, sugar and the sea. This is the story of Fiji.
Some three and a half thousand years ago, the Lapita people, makers of finely decorated pottery, sailed east across open ocean and became the first to settle Fiji.
Later, from the tenth century, the sacred kings of Tonga built a sea power whose influence reached across nearby islands, Fiji among them.
In the 1800s a chief named Cakobau fought his way to power and made himself king of Fiji.
In 1874 Cakobau ceded his islands to Britain. Soon labourers from India were brought in to work the sugar fields, and many stayed.
In 1882 the colony's capital moved to Suva, which remains the capital today.
Kamisese Mara, born in 1920, would become Fiji's first prime minister and lead it for most of its first thirty years.
Sitiveni Rabuka, born in 1948, would be a soldier who seized power, and decades later an elected prime minister.
On the tenth of October 1970, after almost a century of British rule, Fiji became an independent nation.
In 1987 Rabuka led two coups, and Fiji left the Crown to become a republic.
After another crisis in 2000, the army chief Frank Bainimarama took power in a coup in 2006.
Through coups and calm, Fiji remains a meeting place of peoples in the heart of the Pacific.
